theme: Cigarettes, dose → harm (part 2 of 2): other cancers, sexual & reproductive health, eyes, teeth, bones, skin, brain

models.name: Mouth and throat (oral cavity + pharynx) cancer by cigarettes/day
models.estimates: Relative risk of oral and pharyngeal cancer vs never smokers by cigarettes/day, plus fall in risk after quitting (vs continuing).

inputs.name: years_since_quit
inputs.how_we_get_it: date of last cigarette (former smokers only)

models.output_unit: relative risk (pooled RR, random effects; spline points from one-stage dose-response model)

valid_for.population: 115 studies (87 case-control, 28 cohort), published 1969–2024, >40,000 cases, worldwide
valid_for.exposure_range: spline estimated from 20 studies; curve plateaus around RR 5 at 20/day; above ~20/day do not extrapolate upward
valid_for.south_asian_validated: partly: 14 Asian studies give a lower current-smoker RR of 2.26; betel/tobacco-chewing adjustment did not explain the difference

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Substantial heterogeneity (I² ~81%). Publication bias detected for former/ever smokers (not for current). Self-reported smoking.

source.citation: Possenti I, Miotti S, Gallus S, et al. Smoking and oral and pharyngeal cancer: a meta-analysis. Oncol Rev 2026;19:1672607
source.where: Results, 'Dose-response analysis' paragraph; Table 1 (Total and Asia rows); Abstract
source.quote: Estimated RRs were 1.98 (95% CI: 1.74–2.25) for six, 2.88 (95% CI: 2.37–3.50) for ten, and 4.78 (95% CI: 3.64–6.27) for 20 cigarettes/day

supporting_sources.citation: Gandini S, Botteri E, Iodice S, et al. Tobacco smoking and cancer: a meta-analysis. Int J Cancer 2008;122:155-64
supporting_sources.note: Current smokers: oral RR 3.43 (2.37–4.94), pharyngeal RR 6.76 (2.86–15.98). Abstract only.

models.caveats: Supersedes the Doll 2004 mouth/throat/oesophagus table from part 1 for mouth and throat. The spline equation is in Supplementary Box 2 (not opened); only the three printed points are given, so interpolate between them or ask us to pull the spline. In India, chewing tobacco / betel is the bigger driver of mouth cancer (belongs in H2); smoking + alcohol combined effect belongs in H5. Oral cancer alone: current RR 3.39 (2.64–4.35); pharynx alone: 4.24 (2.96–6.09).
models.user_copy: Mouth and throat cancer risk is about {rr} times a non-smoker's at {n} a day (range {lo}–{hi}). It roughly halves within about 10 years of quitting.

models.name: Voice box (larynx) cancer, current smokers
models.estimates: Relative risk of laryngeal cancer in current smokers vs never smokers.

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette logged in last 30 days

valid_for.exposure_range: current vs never; no dose curve in abstract

models.uncertainty: Very wide CI (3.1–15.5); strong heterogeneity by study type, sex and confounder adjustment.

source.citation: Gandini S, Botteri E, Iodice S, Boniol M, Lowenfels AB, Maisonneuve P, Boyle P. Tobacco smoking and cancer: a meta-analysis. Int J Cancer 2008;122(1):155-64
source.quote: Lung (RR = 8.96; 95% CI: 6.73–12.11), laryngeal (RR = 6.98; 95% CI: 3.14–15.52) and pharyngeal (RR = 6.76; 95% CI: 2.86–15.98) cancers presented the highest relative risks (RRs) for current smokers

models.caveats: No dose-response available from this source. Show as 'several times higher' with the wide range, not as a precise number.
models.user_copy: Voice box cancer risk is about 7 times a non-smoker's (wide range: 3–15 times).

models.name: Stomach (gastric) cancer by cigarettes/day and years smoked
models.estimates: Relative risk of gastric cancer vs never smokers by intensity, duration and years since quitting.

valid_for.population: 205 case-control and cohort studies, published up to January 2023, worldwide
valid_for.exposure_range: rises non-linearly up to 20/day, then levels; duration effect linear

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Points between 0 and 20/day are on the non-linear curve in the full paper (not opened).

source.citation: Rota M, Possenti I, Valsassina V, et al. Dose-response association between cigarette smoking and gastric cancer risk: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Gastric Cancer 2024;27(2):197-209
source.quote: GC risk nonlinearly increased with smoking intensity up to 20 cigarettes/day (RR:1.69; 95% CI 1.55-1.84) and levelled thereafter.

models.caveats: H. pylori is the main cause of stomach cancer; smoking adds on top. Free full text is listed at air.unimi.it if you want intermediate curve points.
models.user_copy: Stomach cancer risk is about 1.5 times a non-smoker's (range 1.4–1.6), and about 1.7 times at 20 a day.

models.name: Pancreatic cancer by cigarettes/day
models.estimates: Relative risk of pancreatic cancer vs never smokers by status, intensity, duration and years since quitting.

valid_for.exposure_range: sharp rise at low doses, up to 30/day

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed (rounded to one decimal in abstract).

source.citation: Lugo A, Peveri G, Bosetti C, et al. Strong excess risk of pancreatic cancer for low frequency and duration of cigarette smoking: a comprehensive review and meta-analysis. Eur J Cancer 2018;104:117-126
source.quote: A sharp increase in pancreatic cancer risk was found already with a low number of cigarettes and up to 30 cigarettes/day (RR 2.2, 95% CI: 1.9–2.4).

supporting_sources.citation: Bosetti C et al. Cigarette smoking and pancreatic cancer: an analysis from the International Pancreatic Cancer Case-Control Consortium (PanC4). Ann Oncol 2012;23(7)
supporting_sources.note: Pooled individual data: about twofold risk in current smokers; risk reaches never-smoker level about 20 years after quitting.

models.caveats: Intermediate curve points (e.g. 5 or 10/day) are in the full text only; the abstract says the rise is sharp already at low numbers.
models.user_copy: Pancreatic cancer risk is about 1.8 times a non-smoker's (range 1.7–1.9), even at a few cigarettes a day.

models.name: Kidney cancer by cigarettes/day
models.estimates: Relative risk of kidney cancer vs never smokers at 5 and 30 cigarettes/day and by duration.
models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Risk falls linearly with time since quitting (no numbers in abstract).

source.citation: Liu X, Peveri G, Bosetti C, Bagnardi V, Specchia C, Gallus S, Lugo A. Dose-response relationships between cigarette smoking and kidney cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Crit Rev Oncol Hematol 2019;142:86-93
source.quote: Kidney cancer risk increased non-linearly with smoking intensity, the RR compared with never smokers being 1.18 (95% CI: 1.11–1.26) for five and 1.72 (95% CI: 1.52–1.95) for 30 cigarettes/day

supporting_sources.citation: Hunt JD, van der Hel OL, McMillan GP, Boffetta P, Brennan P. Renal cell carcinoma in relation to cigarette smoking: meta-analysis of 24 studies. Int J Cancer 2005;114:101-8

models.caveats: Two curve points only in the abstract; interpolate on log scale between 5 and 30 as our own step, or pull the spline from full text.
models.user_copy: Kidney cancer risk is about 1.2 times a non-smoker's at 5 a day and about 1.7 times at 30 a day.

models.name: Bladder cancer, current and former smokers
models.estimates: Summary odds ratio of bladder cancer for current and former smokers vs never smokers, with a plateau at ~15/day and 50 pack-years.

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette logged in last 30 days

valid_for.exposure_range: risk plateaus at about 15 cigarettes/day and 50 pack-years

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Dose curve values are in the full text (author manuscript is openly available at the Birmingham URL; only the abstract was read).

source.citation: van Osch FHM, Jochems SHJ, van Schooten FJ, Bryan RT, Zeegers MP. Quantified relations between exposure to tobacco smoking and bladder cancer risk: a meta-analysis of 89 observational studies. Int J Epidemiol 2016;45(3):857-870
source.quote: Current smokers (SOR=3.14, 95% CI=2.53-3.75) and former smokers (SOR=1.83, 95% CI=1.52-2.14) had an increased risk of BC compared to never smokers.

models.caveats: Odds ratios, not RRs; for a relatively rare cancer they approximate RR. Excess risk stays elevated even after long-term quitting (authors), so the H3 recovery copy for bladder should be conservative.
models.user_copy: Bladder cancer risk is about 3 times a non-smoker's (range 2.5–3.8).

models.name: Colorectal (bowel) cancer
models.estimates: Relative risk of colorectal cancer for current and former smokers vs never smokers, with a per-dose slope from an earlier meta-analysis.

valid_for.population: 188 original studies published up to September 2018
valid_for.exposure_range: abstract states risk rises linearly with intensity and duration; slope value not in abstract

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Former > current reflects long latency (risk appears after ~30 years of smoking per Botteri 2008).

source.citation: Botteri E, Borroni E, Sloan EK, et al. Smoking and colorectal cancer risk, overall and by molecular subtypes: a meta-analysis. Am J Gastroenterol 2020;115(12):1940-1949
source.quote: Compared with never smokers, the pooled RR for CRC was 1.14 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.10-1.18) for current smokers and 1.17 (95% CI 1.15-1.20) for former smokers. CRC risk increased linearly with smoking intensity and duration.

supporting_sources.citation: Liang PS, Chen TY, Giovannucci E. Cigarette smoking and colorectal cancer incidence and mortality: systematic review and meta-analysis. Int J Cancer 2009 (PubMed 19142968)
supporting_sources.note: Slope: RR 1.38 for an increase of 40 cigarettes/day; RR 1.51 for an increase of 60 pack-years (CIs not in the snippet read). A separate source, so not merged into the formula.

supporting_sources.citation: Botteri E et al. Smoking and colorectal cancer: a meta-analysis. JAMA 2008;300(23):2765-78
supporting_sources.note: Ever vs never 1.18 (1.11–1.25); association significant only after 30 years of smoking.

models.caveats: Small relative effect; the linear slope from the 2020 paper needs the full text. If you want a per-cigarette line now, Liang 2009 is a single-source option: RR = 1.38^(cigs/40) (our algebra on their printed slope; confirm CI first).
models.user_copy: Bowel cancer risk is about 1.1–1.2 times a non-smoker's, and it builds up over many years of smoking.

models.name: Liver cancer death risk by cigarettes/day
models.estimates: Hazard ratio of dying from liver cancer vs non-smokers, per extra 10 cigarettes/day or 10 pack-years.

valid_for.exposure_range: per-10-cigarette slope from dose-response analysis; range of included doses not stated in abstract

models.uncertainty: Printed as % increase with CI: 7.1% (1.4–13.2) per 10 cigarettes/day; 5.2% (0.02–11.2) per 10 pack-years. Mortality, not incidence.

source.citation: Cigarette smoking increases the risk of mortality from liver cancer: a clinical-based cohort and meta-analysis. J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2015;30(10):1450-1460 (author list not captured in the page I read)
source.quote: The risk increased by 7.1% (95% CI: 1.4-13.2) for per additional 10 cigarettes per day and by 5.2% (95% CI: 0.02-11.2) for per additional 10 pack-years.

supporting_sources.citation: Chuang SC, Lee YC, Hashibe M, et al. Interaction between cigarette smoking and hepatitis B and C virus infection on the risk of liver cancer: a meta-analysis. Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev 2010;19(5):1261-8
supporting_sources.note: Smoking interacts with hepatitis B (more than additive) and C (more than multiplicative) — relevant in India, but no simple number to show.

models.caveats: Coefficients are the printed % converted to multipliers (7.1% → 1.071); no other stitching. Alcohol and hepatitis B/C dominate liver cancer risk; alcohol liver models go in H4.
models.user_copy: Liver cancer death risk is about 1.45 times a non-smoker's (range 1.3–1.6), rising about 7% for every extra 10 a day.

models.name: Cervical cancer (women)
models.estimates: Relative risk of squamous-cell cervical cancer in current and past smokers vs never smokers.

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette logged in last 30 days

valid_for.exposure_range: abstract says squamous risk rises with cigarettes/day and younger starting age (numbers in full text)

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed; stratified by study, age, sexual partners, age at first intercourse, OC use, parity.

source.citation: International Collaboration of Epidemiological Studies of Cervical Cancer (Appleby P, Beral V, et al.). Carcinoma of the cervix and tobacco smoking: collaborative reanalysis of individual data on 13,541 women with carcinoma of the cervix and 23,017 women without carcinoma of the cervix from 23 epidemiological studies. Int J Cancer 2006;118(6):1481-95
source.quote: Current smokers had a significantly increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix compared to never smokers (RR = 1.60 (95% CI: 1.48-1.73), p<0.001).

models.caveats: HPV is the necessary cause; smoking raises risk on top of it. Good hook to pair with 'HPV vaccine / screening' info, not with fear.
models.user_copy: Cervical cancer risk is about 1.6 times a non-smoker's (range 1.5–1.7). Regular screening helps catch it early.

models.name: Breast cancer by cigarettes/day (women)
models.estimates: Relative risk of female breast cancer vs never smokers at 20 and 40 cigarettes/day and by years smoked.
models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Small effect; residual confounding (alcohol) possible.

source.citation: Scala M, Bosetti C, Bagnardi V, et al. Dose-response relationships between cigarette smoking and breast cancer risk: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Epidemiol 2023;33(12):640-8
source.quote: Breast cancer risk increased linearly with intensity of smoking (RR 1.12; 95% CI, 1.08–1.16 for 20 cigarettes/day and 1.26; 95% CI, 1.17–1.36 for 40 cigarettes/day)

models.caveats: Linear, so a per-cigarette formula RR = 1.12^(cigs/20) matches the two printed points closely; this is our algebra on the paper's linear model, please confirm. Alcohol-breast cancer is the bigger lever (H4).
models.user_copy: Breast cancer risk is slightly higher: about +12% at 20 a day (range +8 to +16%).

models.name: Erectile dysfunction, per extra 10 cigarettes/day
models.estimates: Odds ratio of erectile dysfunction for each additional 10 cigarettes/day (and each 10 years of smoking).

valid_for.population: 1 cohort + 9 cross-sectional studies, 50,360 participants, 12,218 cases, searched to March 2014
valid_for.exposure_range: authors found no evidence of curvilinear association; range of doses not given in abstract

models.uncertainty: Mostly cross-sectional data, so causality and reverse causation are less certain; moderate heterogeneity (I² 44.7%) for intensity.

source.citation: Cao S, Gan Y, Dong X, Liu J, Lu Z. Association of quantity and duration of smoking with erectile dysfunction: a dose-response meta-analysis. J Sex Med 2014;11(10):2376-2384
source.quote: The summary odds ratio of ED for an increase of 10 cigarettes smoked per day was 1.14 (95% confidence interval 1.09 to 1.18)

supporting_sources.citation: Cao S, Yin X, Wang Y, Zhou H, Song F, Lu Z. Smoking and risk of erectile dysfunction: systematic review of observational studies with meta-analysis. PLoS One 2013;8(4):e60443
supporting_sources.note: Prospective cohorts only: current smokers OR 1.51 (1.34–1.71), former 1.29 (1.07–1.47).

models.caveats: The formula is the paper's own linear (log-scale) model applied per 10 cigarettes. Sensitive topic: show only if the user opts in to 'sexual health' insights, and never as a diagnosis.
models.user_copy: Erection problems are about +14% more likely for every 10 cigarettes a day (range +9 to +18%).

models.name: Female infertility
models.estimates: Odds of infertility in women who smoke vs non-smokers, and odds of pregnancy per IVF cycle.

inputs.name: sex
inputs.how_we_get_it: profile; show only to women who opt in

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette logged in last 30 days

table.outcome: pregnancy per IVF cycle, smokers vs non-smokers

valid_for.population: 12 studies (infertility) and 9 studies (IVF), published up to 1998
valid_for.exposure_range: smoker vs non-smoker; no dose bands

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Old, observational; the authors flag possible confounding.

source.citation: Augood C, Duckitt K, Templeton AA. Smoking and female infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Hum Reprod 1998;13(6):1532-9
source.quote: the overall value of the odds ratio (OR) for risk of infertility in women smokers versus non-smokers was 1.60 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.34-1.91]

supporting_sources.citation: World Health Organization. Tobacco and infertility (fact document)
supporting_sources.note: Describes the 1998 review as about 1.5 times higher risk, and a newer (unpublished) review at 1.4 times; gives the example 15% → 21%. The newer estimate is cited as unpublished data, so not used as a model.

supporting_sources.citation: Lyngs et al. Female cigarette smoking and successful fertility treatment: a Danish cohort study. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand 2021;100:58-66
supporting_sources.note: In a modern Danish IVF/IUI cohort, occasional/daily smoking was not associated with live birth (RR 1.15, 0.82–1.60). Shows the IVF effect is uncertain.

models.caveats: Show as 'about 1.5 times more likely to have trouble conceiving', never as a personal prediction. Opt-in only.
models.user_copy: Women who smoke are about 1.6 times more likely to have trouble getting pregnant (range 1.3–1.9).

models.name: Male fertility: sperm count
models.estimates: Risk of low sperm count (oligozoospermia) in smoking vs non-smoking men attending infertility care.

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette logged in last 30 days

source.citation: Bundhun PK, Janoo G, Bhurtu A, et al. Tobacco smoking and semen quality in infertile males: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Public Health 2019;19:36
source.quote: Results of this analysis showed oligozoospermia to be significantly higher in smokers (RR: 1.29, 95% CI: 1.05–1.59; P = 0.02).

supporting_sources.citation: Sharma R, Harlev A, Agarwal A, Esteves SC. Cigarette smoking and semen quality: a new meta-analysis examining the effect of the 2010 WHO laboratory methods. Eur Urol 2016;70(4):635-645
supporting_sources.note: 5,865 men; lower sperm count, motility and morphology, larger effect in moderate/heavy smokers. Original not opened; a citing review gives count MD −9.72 ×10^6/ml while another secondary page gives −8.92 — verify against the paper before using any number.

models.caveats: No link to actual time-to-pregnancy for men; do not convert to 'fertility %'.
models.user_copy: In men seeking fertility help, smokers were about 1.3 times more likely to have a low sperm count (range 1.05–1.6).

models.name: Cataract, per 10 pack-years
models.estimates: Relative risk of age-related cataract per 10 pack-years of cumulative smoking, and after quitting.
models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Men only; quitters' lower risk mostly explained by lower total dose.

source.citation: Physicians' Health Study analysis of smoking cessation and age-related cataract in men, JAMA Network (JAMA Ophthalmology archive, article 265801). Full author/year citation not captured in the page I read; please take it from the URL.
source.quote: The reduced risk in past smokers was principally due to a lower total cumulative dose (RR of cataract for increase of 10 pack-years of smoking, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.04-1.10).

supporting_sources.citation: Risk of cataract in smokers: a meta-analysis of observational studies. Arch Soc Esp Oftalmol (Elsevier), abstract
supporting_sources.note: Current smokers, cohort studies: OR 1.41 (1.24–1.60); nuclear cataract OR 1.71 (1.47–1.98).

supporting_sources.citation: Ye J, He J, Wang C, et al. Smoking and risk of age-related cataract: a meta-analysis. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2012;53(7):3885
supporting_sources.note: Current and former smokers at higher risk of nuclear and posterior subcapsular cataract; no association with cortical. Numbers not in the page read.

models.caveats: Cataract is very common in India at older ages; the relative effect is modest. Citation for the primary source needs completing before release (see source.citation).
models.user_copy: Cataract risk goes up about 7% for every 10 pack-years smoked (range 4–10%).

models.name: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD)
models.estimates: Odds of late AMD (neovascular or geographic atrophy) in current and former smokers vs never smokers, aged 65+.

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette logged in last 30 days

models.uncertainty: Wide CIs; cross-sectional; former-smoker value printed as 'around 1.7' without CI.

source.citation: Chakravarthy U, Augood C, Bentham GC, et al. Cigarette smoking and age-related macular degeneration in the EUREYE Study. Ophthalmology 2007;114(6):1157-1163
source.quote: Current smokers had increased odds of neovascular AMD (odds ratio [OR], 2.6; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.4-4.8) or GA (OR, 4.8; 95% CI, 2.1-11.1), whereas for ex-smokers the odds were around 1.7.

supporting_sources.citation: Vingerling JR, Hofman A, Grobbee DE, de Jong PTVM. Age-related macular degeneration and smoking: the Rotterdam Study. Arch Ophthalmol
supporting_sources.note: Under age 85: current smokers 6.6-fold neovascular AMD (2.8–15.9); >10 pack-years RR 6.5 (2.9–14.8); no increased risk 20+ years after quitting.

models.caveats: European, 65+ only; do not show to young users as a number. AMD prevalence and genetics differ in South Asians.
models.user_copy: In older adults, smoking is linked to about 2.5–5 times the risk of the main causes of age-related vision loss.

models.name: Gum disease (periodontitis)
models.estimates: Risk of periodontitis onset or progression in smokers vs non-smokers, and in quitters vs never smokers.

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette logged in last 30 days

valid_for.population: 14 prospective studies (meta-analysis, to May 2017); 6 studies for cessation
valid_for.exposure_range: smoker / quitter / never; no dose slope

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Age explained over half of between-study variation.

source.citation: Leite FRM, Nascimento GG, Scheutz F, López R. Effect of smoking on periodontitis: a systematic review and meta-regression. Am J Prev Med 2018;54(6):831-841
source.quote: Pooled adjusted risk ratios estimate that smoking increases the risk of periodontitis by 85% (risk ratio=1.85, 95% CI=1.5, 2.2).

supporting_sources.citation: Leite FRM, Nascimento GG, Baake S, et al. Impact of smoking cessation on periodontitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective longitudinal observational and interventional studies. Nicotine Tob Res 2018
supporting_sources.note: Source of the quitter rows (RR 0.97 vs never; 1.79 smokers vs quitters). Abstract read via a quitline-association page reproducing it; verify on PubMed (doi 10.1093/ntr/nty147).

models.caveats: Great 'recovery' message for H3: quitters' gum-disease risk was not different from never smokers. Tooth-loss numbers not found this pass.
models.user_copy: Gum disease risk is about 1.85 times a non-smoker's (range 1.5–2.2), and people who quit had about the same risk as never-smokers.

models.name: Bone fractures (any, osteoporotic, hip)
models.estimates: Relative risk of fracture in current smokers vs non-smokers, with and without adjustment for bone density.

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette logged in last 30 days

valid_for.age: older adults (cohort baseline ages vary; mostly 50+)
valid_for.population: 10 prospective cohorts incl. Europe, Canada, USA, Australia, Japan (Hiroshima); 59,232 people, 250,000 person-years

models.uncertainty: The osteoporotic-fracture CI (1.13–1.28) is printed that way in the abstract but does not contain the point estimate 1.29, so it is likely a typo in the original; a secondary summary gives 1.17–1.43. Verify in full text before use.

source.citation: Kanis JA, Johnell O, Oden A, et al. Smoking and fracture risk: a meta-analysis. Osteoporos Int 2005;16(2):155-62
source.quote: The highest risk was observed for hip fracture (RR=1.84; 95% CI=1.52-2.22), but this was also somewhat lower after adjustment for BMD (RR=1.60; 95% CI=1.27-2.02).

models.caveats: This analysis underpins smoking as an input in the FRAX fracture tool (not opened; mention only). Most relevant for users 50+; for young users the absolute risk is tiny.
models.user_copy: Hip fracture risk is about 1.8 times a non-smoker's (range 1.5–2.2), mostly relevant later in life.

models.name: Skin ageing (facial wrinkles)
models.estimates: Relative risk of moderate/severe facial wrinkling in current vs never smokers aged 40+.

inputs.name: is_current_smoker
inputs.how_we_get_it: any cigarette logged in last 30 days

table.group: effect of pack-years in wrinkle score, expressed as years of ageing

models.output_unit: relative risk; years of ageing equivalent
models.uncertainty: Wide CIs; cross-sectional; photo grading. Controlled for age, sun exposure and BMI.

source.citation: Ernster VL, Grady D, Miike R, Black D, Selby J, Kerlikowske K. Facial wrinkling in men and women, by smoking status. Am J Public Health 1995;85:78-82
source.quote: the estimated relative risk of moderate/severe wrinkling for current smokers compared to never smokers was 2.3 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.2, 4.2) among men and 3.1 (95% CI = 1.6, 5.9) among women.

supporting_sources.citation: Koh JS, Kang H, Choi SW, Kim HO. Cigarette smoking associated with premature facial wrinkling: image analysis of facial skin replicas. Int J Dermatol 2002;41(1):21-7
supporting_sources.note: Korean study (Asian skin), 20–69 years: current smokers RR 2.72 (1.32–3.21); >19 pack-years 2.93 (1.14–4.1); 11–19 pack-years 1.75 (1.54–3.67).

models.caveats: Useful motivational hook for young users, but the evidence is small and cross-sectional. The '1.4 years of ageing' figure is the pack-years effect as described in the abstract's words; do not scale it per cigarette.
models.user_copy: People who smoke are about 2–3 times more likely to have noticeable facial wrinkles after 40.

models.name: Dementia, per 20 cigarettes/day
models.estimates: Relative risk of all-cause dementia per 20 cigarettes/day, and for current vs never smokers.

valid_for.age: older adults (cohort baselines mostly 55+; effect strongest at 65–75)
valid_for.exposure_range: dose slope per 20 cigarettes/day; do not extrapolate far above 40/day

models.uncertainty: 95% CIs printed. Competing risk: smokers die earlier, which can bias dementia estimates either way.

models.caveats: Good H3 message: former smokers showed no increased dementia risk (RR 1.01). Show only to users 40+.
models.user_copy: Dementia risk is about +34% for every 20 cigarettes a day (range +25 to +43%), and people who quit had no extra risk.
